passages.text: This is what Peter gives you under a promise of making you sound-minded. For under the pretext of one God he seems to free you from many lifeless idols. These do not do their worshipers much harm, because with their very eyes they can see that they are stone, bronze, gold, or some other lifeless material. Therefore, knowing that what is seen is nothing, the soul cannot be haunted by fear in the same way through the visible thing. But when, through deceptive teaching, it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition. I say these things not because I advise you to revere idols, but because Peter, while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image, introducing a God with a form—and, moreover, supremely just. With this comes terror, and shuddering for the soul that thinks of it, capable even of loosening the tension of sound reasoning. For the mind, placed in such a storm, has its brightness muddied like deep water by a violent wind. Therefore, if he comes for your benefit, let him not, while seeming to dissolve your relatively mild fears arising from lifeless forms, introduce in their place a fearsome form of God. But does God have a form? If he does, he has a shape. If he has a shape, how is he not bounded? If bounded, he is in a place. If in a place, he is less than the place containing him. If less than something, how is he greater, stronger, or higher than all? So much for these matters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς φοβερὸν θεὸν ἀποβλέπουσα τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἐκβαθρεύεται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: when ... it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the upheaval/derangement image and the author’s contrast with nature; this remains Simon’s reported position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὀρθῶν λογισμῶν ἐκλῦσαι τοὺς τόνους
lexical_decisions.chosen: loosening the tension of sound reasoning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the tension image rather than merely saying it makes thinking difficult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μορφὴν δὲ ἔχει θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: form ... shape ... bounded
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps distinct vocabulary in the chain of argument. Bounded denotes spatial delimitation, not simply weakness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φοβερῶν ἰδεῶν δοκῶν ἀπαλλάσσειν ὑμῶν τὰς ψυχάς, φοβερωτέρᾳ ἰδέᾳ τὸν ἑκάστου ὑμῶν ἐνθουσιᾶν ποιεῖ νοῦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδέα can denote form, appearance, or a mental representation. Images preserves the visual thread through idols, imagined forms, and God in a form without asserting that every image is a physical statue. Ideas or conceptions is a material cognitive alternative but would conceal the unqualified visual sense in modern English.

passages.text: It is also obvious that he does not truly believe even the things said by his own teacher, for he proclaims the opposite of them. For, as I learn, his teacher said to someone, “Do not call me good, for the good one is one.” But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one whom the scriptures proclaim, who kills and gives life—kills those who sin and gives life to those who live according to his judgment. That he really did not call the maker good is clear to anyone able to think it through. For the maker was known to Adam, whom he formed; to Enoch, who pleased him; to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous; likewise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and also to Moses, the people, and the whole world. Yet Peter’s teacher Jesus came and said, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father, and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Therefore, if the one present was himself the Son, from his coming he revealed to those he wished the one unknown to all. Thus the Father was unknown to everyone before him, not being this one who was known to all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν, ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do not call me good, for the good one is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the wording actually quoted here, not a familiar expanded Gospel form. Simon’s distinction between good and just is retained as his argument.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δημιουργοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the maker
lexical_decisions.rationale: δημιουργός denotes creator or maker, not automatically an evil demiurge; the speaker’s proposed distinction is not editorially endorsed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δικαίῳ ὁραθέντι Νῶε
lexical_decisions.chosen: to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous
lexical_decisions.rationale: δικαίῳ is taken predicatively, righteous being what God perceived in Noah, fitting the list of people pleasing or accepted by the maker. To righteous Noah, whom he saw is the material attributive alternative: righteousness is then Noah’s epithet rather than the content of the seeing. Both retain Noah as the person seen by God; neither reverses the action into Noah seeing God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinct Greek knew/knows forms instead of homogenizing the quoted tenses.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἰπὼν οὐκέτι ἐκεῖνον λέγει τὸν δίκαιον
lexical_decisions.chosen: But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one
lexical_decisions.rationale: No longer retains the additional οὐκέτι force. It can express the logical consequence under the good designation—no longer under that description—rather than necessarily a chronological change of belief. The clause remains Simon’s argument, not a narrator’s endorsement.

passages.text: And in saying this, Jesus does not even agree with himself. For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God, saying, “Do not fear the one who kills the body but can do nothing to the soul. Fear the one who can cast both body and soul into the Gehenna of fire. Yes, I tell you, fear this one.” That he really said to fear this one as a just God, to whom he also says the wronged should cry out, is shown when he gives a parable on this and adds its explanation, saying, “If, then, the unjust judge acted in this way because he was petitioned repeatedly, how much more will the Father bring vindication for those who cry to him day and night? Or do you think that because he is patient with them, he will not do it? Yes, I tell you, he will do it, and quickly.” But whoever says that God vindicates and repays establishes him as just by nature, and not good. Further, he also gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth. If he is Lord of heaven and earth, he is acknowledged as maker; and being maker, he is just. Calling him good at one time and just at another, he does not agree even in this way. Thirdly, his wise disciple insisted yesterday that direct perception is more adequate than an apparition, not knowing that direct perception can be human, whereas an apparition is acknowledged to belong to divinity.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Gehenna of fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the named place and fire qualification, not the distinct Hades term.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἐκδίκησιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: vindication
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκδίκησις can be vengeance or the securing of justice. Vindication fits the wronged petitioners while retaining the punitive repayment explained afterward.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνάργειαν ὀπτασίας ἱκανωτέραν εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: direct perception is more adequate than an apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνάργεια here is direct evident encounter, contrasted with ὀπτασία, an apparition. The polemical wise disciple is not softened into neutral description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνίοτε γὰρ ἄλλαις φωναῖς τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν φοβερὸν καὶ δίκαιον συνίστησι θεὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν partitively, other statements among those derived from scripture. The subsequent fear, judgment, and Lord-of-heaven-and-earth material continues Simon’s contrast with the scriptural just maker, favoring this reading. The comparative-genitive alternative is with statements different from those from the scriptures; that would distinguish rather than include the statements’ scriptural derivation. The supplied wording permits both and is not emended.

passages.text: “By these and similar statements, Peter, Simon, standing outside and speaking to the crowds, seems to me to be disturbing most of them. So go out immediately and dissolve his false arguments by the power of truth.” After Zacchaeus said this, Peter prayed as usual and went out. He stood in the place of the previous day, greeted the crowds in the customary manner of reverence toward God, and began to speak as follows: “Our Lord Jesus, being a true prophet—as I will also give assurance about this at the proper time—made concise declarations about matters important to the truth, for these two reasons. First, he addressed people who revered God and knew to believe what he uttered as a declaration, for what was said was not foreign to their customary practice. Second, because he had a limited time to proclaim, he did not employ demonstrative argument, so that he might not spend all his allotted time on arguments. Otherwise he would have been occupied with explaining a few statements that could be understood through effort of soul, and would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively. For he declared what he wished as to a people able to understand, among whom we too belong. Whenever, on a rare occasion, we did not understand something he said, we asked him privately, so that none of what he said would remain unintelligible to us.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν πρὸ μιᾶς τόπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the place of the previous day
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical before one refers to one day before; no new location is invented.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ἀποδείξεως οὐκ ἐχρῆτο λόγῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not employ demonstrative argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: Distinguishes concise pronouncement from developed proof, not truthful from untruthful speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπὸ πόνου ψυχῆς νοεῖσθαι δυναμένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: that could be understood through effort of soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the intellectual effort supplied by the source rather than rendering the matters permanently incomprehensible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἀληθείᾳ διαφέροντας μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖον εἰσφέρειν λόγους
lexical_decisions.chosen: would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγους expressly denotes arguments or discourses presented, distinguished from the earlier matters about which declarations were made. Presented retains introducing them into discussion, not simply naming their topics.

passages.text: Knowing, then, that we knew everything he had said and could supply the proofs, when he sent us to the uninstructed nations to baptize them for forgiveness of sins, he commanded us to teach them first. Of these commands, this is the first and great one: to fear the Lord God and serve him alone. The God he said to fear is the one whose angels belonging to the least of the believers among us stand in heaven continually beholding the Father’s face. For he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty, and all his members, not for use. He does not have eyes in order to see from there, for he sees from every side, being in body incomparably brighter than the seeing spirit within us and more radiant than every light, so that compared with him the sun’s light is reckoned darkness. Nor does he have ears in order to hear, for from every side he hears, understands, moves, acts, and makes. He has the most beautiful form for the human being’s sake, so that the pure in heart may be able to see him and rejoice in that for which they endured these things. For with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being, so that the human being might rule and have dominion over all and everything might serve him. Therefore, judging him to be the whole and the human being his image—he himself invisible, but his image, the human being, visible—the one who wishes to revere him honors his visible image, namely the human being. Whatever someone does to a human being, whether good or evil, is referred to him. Therefore judgment from him will go forth to all, assigning to each what is deserved, for it vindicates his form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μορφὴν γὰρ ἔχει διὰ πρῶτον καὶ μόνον κάλλος
lexical_decisions.chosen: he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unusual first/only qualification of beauty. For beauty first and alone is another possible grouping, treating first adverbially; neither reading makes the form a merely metaphorical appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λαμπρότερος ὢν τὸ σῶμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: being in body ... brighter
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the author’s explicit bodily attribution to God without conforming it to a later account of divine incorporeality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ γὰρ αὐτοῦ μορφῇ ὡς ἐν μεγίστῃ σφραγῖδι τὸν ἄνθρωπον διετυπώσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the form/seal/imprint sequence and its relation to human dominion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κρίνας εἶναι τὸ πᾶν αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα τὸν ἄνθρωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: judging him to be the whole and the human being his image
lexical_decisions.rationale: Attaches κρίνας to the following worshipper, whoever wishes to revere him. The worshipper judges God, not himself, to be the whole. Continuing God as subject of a determination from the preceding sentence is a possible contextual alternative: God determined himself to be the whole and the human being his image. The main text chooses the more direct attachment to the following grammatical subject, avoiding a dangling divine determination. The precise God/whole relation is left at the source’s abstract wording, without a later metaphysical explanation.

passages.text: But someone will say, “If he has a form, he also has a shape and is in a place. If he is in a place and contained by it as something lesser, how is he great above all? And how can he be everywhere while having a shape?” To the person saying this, one can first say: those around Simon persuade people to believe such thoughts about him; but we know to be true the things attested by our Lord Jesus Christ. We are not obliged to provide you at a command with proofs that things are so. But first I will speak about place and God. Place is what does not exist, whereas God is what exists; and what does not exist cannot be compared with what exists. For how can place have existence, unless it is a second region, such as heaven, earth, water, air, or any other body, which would also fill the void there? It is called void for this reason: because it is nothing. Nothing is a more suitable name for it. For what is the so-called void—some sort of vessel that contains nothing? Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, if it is a vessel, place is that in which the empty vessel itself is. For what exists must necessarily be in what is nothing. This is what I mean by what does not exist, which some call place: it is nothing. How can what is nothing be compared with what exists, except as opposites, so that what exists is not called place, but what does not exist is? But even if it is something, although many examples press to come forth from me as proof, I wish to use just one, to show that what contains is not invariably stronger than what is contained. The sun is a circular shape and is wholly contained by air, but it illuminates the air, heats it, and cuts through it. When the sun is absent from it, the air is enveloped in darkness, and wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying. But at the sun’s rising it is illuminated again, and wherever it is warmed by the sun it is also adorned with greater beauty. The sun does these things by its presence, although its substance is bounded. What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and everything, from himself having shape, form, and beauty, while the presence proceeding from him extends infinitely?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀληθεῖς γινώσκομεν τὰς μαρτυρουμένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: we know to be true the things attested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine plural has no expressed noun; things or statements attested expresses the ellipsis without adding an extra source claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὲν ὂν μὴ ᾖ, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τόπος λέγηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: what exists is not called place, but what does not exist is
lexical_decisions.rationale: Understands place from the second clause as the predicate to the first, not an assertion that what exists ceases to exist.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording says bright, not dark. The resulting physical description is puzzling, but the main text preserves that printed adjective rather than silently emending it to fit the argument. Its referent is understood as a part of the air.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ μετουσίαν ἀπείρως ἐκτεταμένην ἔχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the presence proceeding from him extends infinitely
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετουσία can be presence, participation, or communicated influence. Presence preserves the analogy with the bounded sun’s effects without adding a second bodily substance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ ἂν καὶ αὐτοῦ πληροῦν τὸ κενόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: which would also fill the void there
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes αὐτοῦ locatively, there, referring to the discussed place or region. It is not nominative emphatic αὐτό, itself. A genitive alternative is which would also fill its void, with the precise possessive referent drawn from the surrounding body/region discussion; no replacement Greek is adopted.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
source_issues.issue: The wording associates becoming bright with cooling, which is puzzling in this analogy. Bright is nevertheless what the supplied text says; no emendation to dark has been made.

passages.text: This is the mystery of the sevenfold order. For he himself is the rest of all things, so that to those who imitate his greatness on a small scale he grants himself as rest. He alone is in one respect graspable and in another ungraspable, in one respect bounded and in another unbounded, having the extensions from him reaching into infinity. For he is graspable and ungraspable, near and far, being here and there, existing alone and possessing the communicating presence of the mind that is infinite on every side. By breathing this, the souls of all have life. Even if they are separated from the body, if they are found to possess longing for him, they are carried immortal into his embrace, just as in winter the vapors of the mountains, drawn by the sun’s rays, are carried toward the sun. What affection, then, can we conceive if we behold the beauty of his form with our mind? Otherwise it is impossible: for beauty cannot exist without form, nor can anyone be drawn toward love of him or even imagine seeing God if he has no form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑβδομάδος μυστήριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: mystery of the sevenfold order
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑβδομάς is a group of seven or a week. Sevenfold order retains the six extensions plus rest discussed just before; mystery of the week is a viable more familiar alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ πανταχόθεν ἀπείρου νοὸς τὴν μετουσίαν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: possessing the communicating presence of the mind that is infinite on every side
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετουσία can be participation, presence, or shared influence. Communicating presence retains its life-imparting reach in the breathing clause, without silently identifying a second deity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: they are carried ... into his embrace
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόλπος is bosom or lap; embrace makes the intimate image readable while retaining a personal destination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: just as in winter the vapors of the mountains
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the vapor simile and its mountain origin, without a modern scientific correction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ κόλπον φέρονται, ὡς ἐν χειμῶνι ὥρας οἱ ἀτμοὶ τῶν ὀρῶν ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἡλίου ἀκτίνων ἑλκόμενοι φέρονται πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀθάνατοι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: they are carried immortal into his embrace, just as in winter the vapors of the mountains, drawn by the sun’s rays, are carried toward the sun
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches immortal to the souls because the paragraph concerns their continued life after separation from the body. ἀθάνατοι can grammatically agree with feminine souls or masculine vapors, and its printed position after the simile permits the local alternative the vapors ... are carried toward the sun, immortal. Moving the adjective to the souls is a disclosed attachment choice, not uniquely established by morphology.

passages.text: Peter said, “You proposed to speak to one point but answered another. For you proposed that someone is better able to understand more ...... by hearing from an apparition than, indeed, from direct perception ... But then you went on to persuade us that the person hearing from an apparition is more secure than the one hearing from direct perception itself. Indeed, this was why you asserted that you knew Jesus’ teachings more adequately than I, as someone who had heard the word from him through an apparition. Nevertheless I answer the point proposed at the beginning. Once the prophet has first given assurance that he is a prophet, he is securely believed concerning what he says directly; having first been recognized as truthful, he answers after being examined and questioned as the learner wishes. But someone who trusts an apparition, a vision, or a dream is in danger, for he does not know whom he trusts. It is possible that this is an evil demon or a deceptive spirit, pretending in its speech to be what it is not. If someone should wish to inquire who the one appearing is, the apparition can say whatever it wishes about itself. Thus, flashing like an evil being and remaining as long as it wishes, it is extinguished, without staying for the questioner’s examination as long as the questioner wanted. Someone who sees through dreams cannot even inquire about what he wishes, for the sleeper’s reasoning is not under his own control. This is why, though we desire to learn many things while awake, in a dream we ask about other things, or, without even asking, hear about things of no concern to us. On waking we are discouraged that we neither heard about nor examined what we desired to learn.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ...
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone is better able to understand more ...... by hearing from an apparition than, indeed, from direct perception ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: Better able separately represents μᾶλλον with δύνασθαι, while understand more represents πλεῖον with νοεῖν. Exactly six and three printed gap dots remain; no missing words are restored. The comparison is retained, with indeed representing γάρ in the interrupted construction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δύναται λέγειν ἑαυτῷ ὃ βούλεται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: the apparition can say whatever it wishes about itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of δύναται is unstated. The main text takes the apparition as subject, interpreting the dative as speaking on its own behalf, with self-description inferred from the preceding identity question. About itself is not claimed as the literal meaning of ἑαυτῷ. A materially different reading takes the questioner as subject and the reflexive as to himself: If someone wishes to inquire who the appearing figure is, he can tell himself whatever he wishes. The following evanescent apparition favors the main subject continuation, but does not eliminate the alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ δαίμονα κακὸν εἶναι ἢ πνεῦμα πλάνον
lexical_decisions.chosen: an evil demon or a deceptive spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both alternatives remain distinct.

source_issues.source_quote: μᾶλλον δύνασθαί τινα πλεῖον νοεῖν ...... παρ’ ὀπτασίας ἀκούοντα, ἢ γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἐναργείας ...
source_issues.issue: Six dots and then three dots mark two printed gaps. Both exact counts remain, without restoring the missing wording or hiding the interrupted syntax.

passages.text: Simon said, “If you say that apparitions do not always speak truth, nevertheless visions and dreams, being sent by God, do not lie about whatever he wishes to say.” Peter said, “You said correctly that, being sent by God, they do not lie. But it is unclear whether the person who saw it has seen a God-sent dream.” Simon said, “If the person who saw it is righteous, he has seen something true.” Peter said, “You said correctly. But who is righteous if he needs a vision to learn what he ought to learn and to do what he ought to do?” Simon said, “Grant me this, that only the righteous person can see a true vision, and I will answer you on that point. For I have decided that an impious person does not see a true dream.” Peter said, “This is false, and I can demonstrate it both without writing and from writing, though I do not promise to persuade you. For a man who has inclined toward love of a wicked woman does not transfer his mind to lawful life together with another who is good in every way. Sometimes, even knowing in themselves which is better, because they are already captivated they love the worse one. You too are suffering something like this without knowing it.” Simon said, “Leave these things aside and speak to what you promised. For it seems impossible to me for impious people to be given dreams by God in any manner.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγράφως καὶ ἐγγράφως
lexical_decisions.chosen: both without writing and from writing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between proof apart from written texts and proof from them, not between illiteracy and literacy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προειλημμένοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: because they are already captivated
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preoccupation or prior capture explains the persistence in an inferior attachment; no explicit compulsion beyond the source is added.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὖν γε τὰ ὁράματα καὶ τὰ ἐνύπνια θεόπεμπτα ὄντα οὐ ψεύδεται, περὶ ὧν ἂν εἰπεῖν θέλῃ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: nevertheless visions and dreams, being sent by God, do not lie about whatever he wishes to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: He understands God as the subject of θέλῃ, chosen because God is the sender encoded in θεόπεμπτα. The subject is not expressly named. About whatever they wish to say is a material alternative with visions and dreams as subject, since a neuter plural can take a singular verb, as the immediately preceding ψεύδεται does. Neither reading requires correcting the supplied text.

passages.text: Nevertheless, that even impious people see true visions and dreams is clear, and I can prove it from writing. For it is written in the law that Abimelech—being impious and having wished to defile the wife of righteous Abraham through intercourse—heard from God in sleep, as the scripture says, not to touch her because she was living with a husband. Pharaoh too, an impious man, saw a dream about abundance and scarcity of wheat; Joseph, explaining it to him, said that the dream had come from God. Nebuchadnezzar, who revered idols and ordered those who revered God to be thrown into fire, saw a dream concerning an age’s whole length. And let no one say, “But no impious person beholds a vision while awake.” That is false. Nebuchadnezzar himself, after ordering three men to be thrown into fire, saw a fourth in the furnace and said, “I see the fourth as a son of God.” Yet although they saw true apparitions, visions, and dreams, they were impious. Such a person is not necessarily reverent simply because he sees visions, dreams, and apparitions. For to the reverent person truth wells up in an inborn and pure mind, not pursued through a dream, but given to good people through understanding.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τέταρτον ὁρῶ ὡς υἱὸν θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: I see the fourth as a son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the anarthrous son of God in the quoted statement without identifying the figure as a particular later doctrinal person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὄνειρον ὅλου μήκους αἰῶνος
lexical_decisions.chosen: a dream concerning an age’s whole length
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the broad age-duration wording rather than identifying an unprinted historical timetable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ εὐσεβεῖ ἐμφύτῳ καὶ καθαρῷ ἀναβλύζει τῷ νῷ τὸ ἀληθές
lexical_decisions.chosen: to the reverent person truth wells up in an inborn and pure mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjectival grouping can also be taken as in the reverent, inborn, and pure mind; both emphasize inward truth and do not make the dream the source of it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνιδὼν τῇ καμίνῳ τέταρτον ἔφη
lexical_decisions.chosen: saw a fourth in the furnace and said
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέταρτον remains the object of seeing in the narrator’s construction, not merely the subject matter of the subsequent speaking. The following quotation is retained as a separate reported statement.

passages.text: If, then, our Jesus also appeared to you through a vision, was made known, and conversed with you, it was as with an adversary, in anger. That is why he spoke through visions and dreams, or even through revelations that come from outside. But can anyone become wise for teaching through an apparition? If you say, “It is possible,” why did the teacher remain and converse with people who were awake for an entire year? And how shall we even believe you about the very claim that he appeared to you? How did he appear to you, when you think the opposite of his teaching? But if, after being seen and instructed by him for a single hour, you became an apostle, proclaim his words, explain his teachings, love his apostles, and do not fight me, who lived with him. For you have stood against me as an enemy, when I am a solid rock, a foundation of an assembly. If you were not an adversary, you would not, by slandering me, revile the proclamation that comes through me, so that I should not be believed when I say what I myself heard from the Lord while present—that is, as though I had been condemned and were unapproved. Or if you call me “condemned,” you accuse the God who revealed the Messiah to me and attack the one who pronounced me blessed on account of revelation. But if you truly wish to cooperate with the truth, first learn from us what we learned from him, and, becoming a disciple of truth, become our fellow worker.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπ’ ἐκείνου μιᾶς ὥρας ὀφθεὶς καὶ μαθητευθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being seen and instructed by him for a single hour
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the passive being seen by him rather than silently reversing it into seeing him. The hour qualifies the short encounter and instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: στερεὰν πέτραν ὄντα με, θεμέλιον ἐκκλησίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: when I am a solid rock, a foundation of an assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Peter’s self-description as rock/foundation. Church is a conventional alternative for ἐκκλησία, but the Greek does not specify a later institution.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν χριστὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB title rendering because χριστός here functions independently, not in a personal-name construction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: „κατεγνωσμένον“
lexical_decisions.chosen: “condemned”
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the marked quoted verdict without identifying an unnamed opponent with a historical person not named in this section.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δηλονότι ὡς ἐμοῦ καταγνωσθέντος καὶ ἐμοῦ ἀδοκίμου ὄντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: —that is, as though I had been condemned and were unapproved
lexical_decisions.rationale: δηλονότι introduces an explanatory statement of the alleged grounds for withholding belief. That is preserves its scope outside the supposed condemnation rather than saying that condemnation itself was clear.

passages.text: Hearing this, Simon said, “Far be it from me to become a disciple either of him or of you. For I am not ignorant of what must be known. What I asked about as though learning was so that I might know whether you can show evidence to be more evident than an apparition. But you spoke as you wished; you did not demonstrate it. And now, tomorrow, I will come and speak with you on the subject of God, whom you insist is the maker, and show that he is not the highest and good. I will also show that your teacher said the same things as I, and expose you as not having understood.” After saying this, he went out, unwilling to hear an answer to the matters he had proposed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀπτασίας ἐνάργειαν ἐναργεστέραν δεῖξαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: show evidence to be more evident than an apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Evidence/evident preserves the visible repetition of ἐνάργεια/ἐναργεστέρα. Evidence here denotes manifest direct encounter, the direct-perception category contrasted earlier with apparition, not documentary or syllogistic proof. ὀπτασίας is taken as the comparative genitive, than an apparition, because Simon asks whether Peter can establish the superiority of direct encounter. The material possessive alternative takes it with ἐνάργειαν: show more evident manifestation of an apparition, with the comparison left implicit. Neither attachment is a correction to the printed Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ αὐτὸν εἶναι ἀνώτατον καὶ ἀγαθόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he is not the highest and good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the coordinated predicate under the negative without silently splitting it into two independent categorical denials.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σὺ δὲ ὡς ἠθέλησας εἶπες, οὐχ ἔδειξας.
lexical_decisions.chosen: But you spoke as you wished; you did not demonstrate it.
lexical_decisions.rationale: As represents the manner expressed by ὡς, not an object meaning whatever content you wished. The contrasting failure to demonstrate remains explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὸν σὸν δὲ διδάσκαλον τὰ αὐτά μοι εἰρηκέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will also show that your teacher said the same things as I
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes μοι as a dative of comparison with the same things, because Simon proposes to prove the teacher’s agreement with his asserted position against Peter’s interpretation. The same things to me is a material alternative taking μοι as recipient of said; the main rendering does not claim that Simon’s receipt of teaching is grammatically excluded.
